title: After Hormuz: Will the Houthis Block Another Chokepoint?
transcriptText:
On March the 28th, the Houthis joined
the war in the Middle East, firing
missiles at Israel.
Iranian officials had long threatened to
unleash their Yemeni proxy if the United
States and Israel escalated. And the
Houthis themselves have said that their
fingers were on the trigger.
But they have not yet played one of the
most important cards still at their
disposal. Attacking shipping in the Bab
al-Mandab choke point.
This would block the Middle East's other
strategic choke point.
Perhaps they feel too weak to do so
after the large-scale US and Israeli
strikes against them last year.
Perhaps they've been incentivized to
stay out of the conflict. Could the
Saudis have paid them off?
Or perhaps they are just biding their
time and waiting until Iran faces even
more pressure before beginning their
attacks.
There are some signs that we might be
heading towards that option.
Even though talks are reportedly ongoing
between the United States and Iran, the
Trump administration has sent thousands
of ground troops to the region ahead of
a potential land invasion of Iran.
And President Trump has also threatened
widespread attacks against Iran's energy
and water infrastructure.
What's clear is that if we think trade
disruption and energy prices are bad
now, they will get much worse if the
Houthis do block another choke point.
Let me explain why.
So, the Strait of Hormuz over here has
got a lot of attention in recent weeks.
Of course, Iran has decided to block
that to most ships. And that
traditionally would carry a huge amount
of global energy flows. Before this
conflict, something like 23.2 million
barrels per day. But what gets a lot
less attention is this other choke point
that is down here between Yemen on the
Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti in the
Horn of Africa.
And that choke point sees a smaller
volume of global energy trade, but it's
still really important. Last year, it
was something like 4.2 million barrels
per day. Now, that actually went down in
recent years because the Houthis
attacked it
in 2023.
This is after the October the 7th
attacks
and the Houthis responded to Israel's
invasion of Gaza. If we look at this
graph, it shows
what happened to energy flows going
through Bab al-Mandab
after 2023 when the Houthis started
attacking. You can see that the amount
going through both Bab al-Mandab and
also the Suez Canal in Egypt goes way
down.
And then in to make up for it, ships
started diverting around the Cape of
Good Hope in Africa. So, you can see the
amount of oil transported through the
Cape of Good Hope goes up after 2023.
So, this is something that Houthis have
already done and that has real
implications for maritime trade.
Let's think about container
shipment. So, if we take a hypothetical
journey from Mumbai in India to Rome in
Italy. Normally, that would go through
Bab al-Mandab and
through the Red Sea up through the Suez
Canal into the Mediterranean before
going on to Rome. And that journey would
have taken about 18 days. Now, if it
would have to go all the way around
Africa, round the Cape of Good Hope, up
past Spain into the Mediterranean that
way, it would take more than twice as
long. That's 44 days on average. And so,
of course, that means trade is slower,
but it also means it's much more
expensive.
And so, that has real implications on
the global economy.
Now, let's think about what this means
for Saudi Arabia. So, Saudi Arabia, of
course, is a major exporter of oil. And
traditionally, it would send a lot of
its oil through the Strait of Hormuz
from its oil fields on the eastern
coast.
Now, it doesn't have that option
anymore. And so, luckily, it had a
mitigation strategy.
They had built a major pipeline from the
east to the west. You can see
the journey it takes. Which was a
mitigation strategy. So, this was
started to be built in the 1980s. And
the idea was that if the Strait of
Hormuz was ever blocked, they could
divert their oil exports
to the western coast of Saudi Arabia and
export it through the Red Sea.
So,
that pipeline has a maximum capacity of
about 5 million barrels per day. And it
comes out at a port on the western coast
called Yanbu.
And it is already operating at maximum
capacity.
Now, if we think about where that oil
goes, we have a sense of who might be
affected if the Houthis really do close
that close Bab al-Mandab down here.
Because nearly all of
the oil exports
from Saudi Arabia go to Asia.
We can see about 23% go to China, 14% to
Japan, South Korea, and India. And only
25% go to the rest of the world.
So, that means that it really would have
a very significant effect on states in
Asia.
And and they would likely suffer most of
the consequences of this.
But it would also have an impact on some
other vulnerable states. And one of
those that's important to think about is
Egypt. So, if we go back to this map, we
can see that of course Egypt has the
Suez Canal connecting the Red Sea to the
Mediterranean. And it also has a
pipeline called the Sumed pipeline,
which connects
into the Mediterranean as well.
So,
this isn't just about
oil though. This is also about the
disruption of maritime trade.
Because this would
have a major consequence for Egypt and
its economy. So far, Egypt has actually
not been involved directly in the
conflict. It has managed to insulate
itself from that.
But the consequences of losing revenue
stream from the Suez Canal would be
major.
30% of global container traffic
typically passes through the Suez Canal.
And this is a major source of foreign
revenue reserves for Egypt. It In back
in 2023, it generated as much as 9.4
billion dollars in foreign reserves for
Egypt. And so, the loss of those
revenues would come at a time of real
fragility for Egypt. They are very
vulnerable because of a pre-existing
financial crisis. The Egyptian pound has
already depreciated and that has several
knock-on effects. First, the government
is unable to afford to pay the subsidies
of fuel and basic goods that it
typically provides.
So, we can see that even in just the
first few weeks of Egypt, there was a
huge spike in fuel prices in Egypt.
And this is different kinds of fuel as
well. It's not just about
transportation, it's also fuel
for cooking
and for heating and cooling as well.
So,
we see, you know, butane gas cylinders
rose as much as 22% in just a few weeks.
So, what the Egyptian government has had
to do is begin energy rationing. And
they have actually started to close
businesses at night. So, they have said
all businesses in Egypt have to close
after 9:00 p.m. And that has a major
impact on Egypt and and on Egyptians
because of course, we're heading towards
the summer. It's getting hotter and a
lot of economic activity, but also
social life takes place in the evenings.
So, now people can't go out to
businesses in the evening. And the
government has also said things like
civil servants have to work remotely at
times.
And and there are real concerns that
they're going to have to take even more
extreme measures.
It's also impacting food prices though.
And food is also something that is
heavily subsidized by the Egyptian
government.
You can see here that the price for the
merchant price for things like flour
have gone up nearly 13% already.
Wheat feed as well. But this is also
affecting consumers. So, we can see a
kilogram of potatoes. That's up nearly
or up 32%.
Tomatoes, the same thing. Unsubsidized
bread as well. And these numbers come
from my colleague Anna Eavey who's
actually in Egypt right now.
And so, what this means is that the
crisis is already hitting the poorest
Egyptians and even those in the middle
classes. And so, if the Bab al-Mandab
was closed by the Houthis, all of this
would get times worse. And as conditions
worsen in Egypt, we could see really
major spillover effects elsewhere. We
often think about Egypt as being too big
to fail. It's a country of 120 million
inhabitants. But if living conditions
worsen, could we see new waves of
migrant outflows? Could the stability of
the regime itself be challenged?
So, it's no longer hyperbole to consider
these potential consequences.
And Egypt is just one of many countries
around the world that would be plunged
into crisis if the Houthis do try to
block Bab-el-Mandeb.
And this is a picture from mid-March, uh
a rally in the capital of Yemen, Sana'a,
where they threatened to do exactly
that. If they do, the ripple effects
will be wide-reaching.
As of today, we still don't know if they
will actually get involved or not. But
what's clear is that if they do, the
costs of the war for the global economy
will rise considerably. And some
governments will have to resort to even
more drastic measures to weather the
storm.
>> [music]
